review.notes: Built on the course: KRAs, SMART, KPI cards, leading vs lagging, weighted score incl. lower-is-better, OKR outcomes and scoring, SBI, feedforward, performance log, rating biases, calibration, Mager and Pipe causes, PIP. Calculations checked. Fictional company.

content.company: Crestline Drinks (fictional), a beverage company with a team of 8 sales reps
content.briefing: It is year-end review season. You must score your 8 reps fairly, defend your ratings in calibration, set next year's goals, and deal with one rep who is falling behind. HR will check every rating against evidence.

variants.text: Rep Joana: sales 90 of 100 target (weight 50%), order errors 2.5 against a target of 2.0, lower is better (weight 30%), new outlets 100% of target (weight 20%). Her weighted score?

choices.f: You scored errors as 2.5 / 2.0 = 125%, which rewards more errors. For lower-is-better KPIs use target / actual.
That is a simple average of 90, 80 and 100. Apply the weights.

variants.text: Rep Paulo: sales 110 of 100 target (weight 60%), visits 80% of target (weight 40%). His weighted score?

choices.f: That is the simple average. Weights matter.
You added the achievements without weights.

variants.text: Two reps argue: one counts 'active outlets' as any outlet that ordered this year, the other only those that ordered this month.

choices.t: Write a KPI card: formula, source, owner, target
choices.f: The card ends the argument. Everyone measures the same way.

choices.t: Let each rep use their own definition
choices.f: Scores become impossible to compare.

choices.t: Pick the definition that gives higher scores
choices.f: That inflates results and fails calibration.

variants.text: Next year's goal for a rep: 'Run a promotion in the Lobito area.' How do you improve it?

choices.t: Make it an outcome: active outlets from 80 to 110
choices.f: Outcomes, not tasks. The promotion becomes one way to reach it.

choices.t: Add the date and budget for the promotion
choices.f: Better, but still a task. Success is the result, not the activity.

choices.t: Keep it; it is clear and easy to check
choices.f: Running a promotion that changes nothing would count as success.

variants.text: Key result: active outlets from 80 (start) to 110 (target). It is now 101. What is the OKR score?

choices.f: That is 101 / 110, which ignores the start.
That is the gain divided by 100, not by the planned gain.

variants.text: Which of these is a leading indicator for monthly sales?

choices.t: Customer visits made per week
choices.f: Activities that predict results. You can act on it mid-month.

choices.t: Monthly sales revenue
choices.f: That is the lagging result itself.

choices.t: Last year's annual market share
choices.f: A lagging measure, and an old one.

variants.text: In March, Joana handled a supermarket buyer's complaint very well. It is now December.

choices.t: Your log has the date, behaviour and impact
choices.f: Notes written close to the event protect her rating from recency bias.

choices.t: You remember it roughly; that is enough
choices.f: Memory favours recent events. March fades.

choices.t: Ask Joana to remind you of her good work
choices.f: A self-assessment helps, but your own evidence matters most.

variants.text: Paulo was rude to a customer at yesterday's visit. When do you raise it?

choices.t: This week, using SBI
choices.f: Feedback close to the event. He apologises to the customer.

choices.t: In the year-end review
choices.f: Months late. Problems grow when nobody speaks.

choices.t: Only if the customer complains
choices.f: You saw it. Waiting signals it is acceptable.

variants.text: A rep keeps missing stock checks. You want to help without judging his past. Which approach?

choices.t: Feedforward: ask what he could do next time
choices.f: Suggestions about the future, not criticism of the past. He proposes a checklist.

choices.t: List every missed check this year
choices.f: Pure criticism of the past. He gets defensive.

choices.t: Wait for the year-end review
choices.f: The problem continues all year.

variants.text: How do you run your weekly one-to-ones with the reps?

choices.t: Their agenda first, then KPIs and obstacles
choices.f: Short, regular, employee-led. Issues surface early.

choices.t: Only a review of last week's numbers
choices.f: A numbers check misses obstacles and feedback.

choices.t: Once a quarter, for one long session
choices.f: Too rare. Problems wait months.

variants.text: Joana had a weak first half but an excellent December. You want to rate her 'Exceeds'. What bias risk?

choices.t: Recency: check the whole year in your log
choices.f: A good December can hide a weak year. The log shows 'Meets' is fair.

choices.t: Halo: she is popular with the team
choices.f: Popularity is not mentioned. This is about timing.

choices.t: No bias: December counts the most
choices.f: All twelve months count equally.

variants.text: Paulo is brilliant with customers, so you rate him high on admin too, though his reports are often late.

choices.t: Halo: rate each area on its own evidence
choices.f: One strength made everything look good. You rate admin 'Below'.

choices.t: Fair: strong reps deserve good scores
choices.f: Halo bias. Calibration will challenge it.

choices.t: Contrast: compare him to the weakest rep
choices.f: That is another bias. Rate against the standard.

variants.text: You rated all 8 reps 'Meets'. HR questions it.

choices.t: Central tendency: re-rate on the evidence
choices.f: Everyone in the middle hides real differences. Two reps clearly exceed.

choices.t: It is fair; they are all similar
choices.f: The KPI data shows wide differences.

choices.t: Raise all to 'Exceeds' to motivate
choices.f: Leniency bias. Ratings lose meaning.

variants.text: In calibration, another manager says your rep should drop a level. What do you bring?

choices.t: Evidence: scorecard and log notes
choices.f: Ratings backed by evidence survive calibration.

choices.t: Your strong personal opinion
choices.f: Opinions lose to evidence.

choices.t: Agree, to keep the meeting short
choices.f: The rep loses a fair rating to save time.

variants.text: Rep Mário's sales fell for 3 months. Before acting, what do you check?

choices.t: Whether he can't, is blocked, or won't
choices.f: His tablet has been broken for 3 months. The cause is blocked, not won't.

choices.t: Start a PIP to show you are serious
choices.f: A PIP without diagnosis treats the wrong cause.

choices.t: Move him to a smaller territory
choices.f: Possible later, but diagnose first.

variants.text: A rep knows the visit standard, could do it, has tools, but skips visits to go home early.

choices.t: Won't: a clear conversation and consequences
choices.f: Motivation or conduct. Training would not help.

choices.t: Can't: send him to sales training
choices.f: He has the skills already.

choices.t: Blocked: give him a better vehicle
choices.f: Nothing blocks him.

variants.text: After coaching, the gap continues. You write a PIP. What must it include?

choices.t: Gap with evidence, SMART targets, support, dates
choices.f: No PIP without real support. He knows exactly what success means.

choices.t: A warning that he will be dismissed
choices.f: A PIP aims at improvement, not just paperwork.

choices.t: A general target to 'try harder'
choices.f: Vague targets cannot be met or measured.

variants.text: What is the right order of escalation for a performance gap?

choices.t: Informal talk, coaching, PIP, then HR process
choices.f: Each step is recorded. The process is fair and defensible.

choices.t: PIP first, then talk if he objects
choices.f: Starting with a PIP skips the earlier, fairer steps.

choices.t: Straight to HR for a formal process
choices.f: Skipping steps is unfair and often against procedure.

variants.text: How should the final rating split results and behaviours?

choices.t: Both, weighted, e.g. 70% results, 30% how
choices.f: A rep who hits target by misleading customers should not get top marks.

choices.t: Results only: sales are what matter
choices.f: How results are achieved also matters.

choices.t: Behaviours only: results depend on luck
choices.f: Results are the main purpose of the job.

variants.text: You tend to rate higher the reps who went to your old university. What bias, and what do you do?

choices.t: Similar-to-me: test each rating on evidence
choices.f: Ask: would I rate this the same for someone different?

choices.t: Contrast: compare them with one another
choices.f: Contrast is judging against the previous person.

choices.t: Central tendency: give everyone the middle
choices.f: A different bias. The issue is favouring people like you.
